chief_complaint: Widespread exfoliating rash and systemic unwellness with signs of sepsis.
history_of_present_illness: The patient's family reported she had become increasingly withdrawn and was not getting out of the house much at all. She presented with a widespread exfoliative rash involving all limbs, especially the armpits, buttocks and thighs, with many flakes of skin covering her mattress and fissures over her wrists and knees. She also appeared pale, clammy and poorly responsive.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in a crowded back room in a remote indigenous community in tropical northern Australia, where scabies remains endemic. Many household members, particularly children, had multiple scabies lesions with secondary pyoderma, indicating the patient may have been a 'core transmitter' of scabies in the community.
vitals: Temperature 39.5°C (103.1°F), heart rate 110bpm, respiratory rate 28 breath cycles per minute, blood pressure 85 mmHg systolic to radial pulsation, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. After IV fluids, her blood pressure rose to 95 mmHg systolic and oxygen saturation was 97% with oxygen by nasal prongs.
physical_exam: The patient presented with a widespread exfoliative rash involving all limbs, armpits, buttocks, and thighs, with many flakes of skin covering the mattress. Fissures were noted over her wrists and knees. She looked pale, clammy, and poorly responsive. Thick deposits of debris with mites often accumulate beneath thickened and dystrophic nails in such cases. The distribution of crusted scabies can be extensive, including the neck, face, scalp, axillae, trunk, buttocks, and limbs, especially knees and elbows. The presence of itch is variable in crusted scabies, unlike ordinary scabies.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory work-up included blood cultures, full blood count, CRP, biochemistry, and skin scrapings. Microscopy of skin scrapings confirmed the diagnosis by showing multiple scabies mites of varying maturity and eggs. Blood cultures taken in the community grew S. aureus resistant to flucloxacillin and clindamycin, but sensitive to gentamicin, co-trimoxazole and doxycycline (community-acquired MRSA). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no features of endocarditis. Repeated blood cultures 48 hours after admission were negative. Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common, and serum IgE levels are often extremely high in crusted scabies cases.
differential_diagnosis: The provisional diagnosis was crusted scabies, with secondary sepsis likely from Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes bacteraemia due to inoculation through skin fissures, though Gram-negative or polymicrobial sepsis was also considered. The differential diagnoses of crusted scabies also include psoriasis, extensive tinea corporis, skin malignancies such as T-cell lymphomas (mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome), nutritional deficiencies (pellagra), pemphigus, kava dermopathy, onchocerciasis, lepromatous leprosy and secondary syphilis.
management_and_clinical_course: Initial management involved transport to a community health centre, oxygen administration, insertion of a wide-bore cannula, additional blood cultures, 1 litre of normal saline over 30 minutes, and commencement of intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone 2g and gentamicin 320mg (for a 62kg patient). After IV fluids, blood pressure rose and oxygen saturation improved. The patient was evacuated to a regional hospital, managed in a single room with enhanced contact precautions. Treatment consisted of a five-dose course of ivermectin (200 µg/kg/dose) on days 0, 1, 7, 8 and 14, and topical benzyl benzoate 25% applied every second day for the first week, then twice weekly for the second week. A keratolytic cream (lactic acid and urea in sorbolene cream) was applied after bathing on days without topical scabicide. Due to MRSA findings, IV vancomycin was administered for 2 weeks. She became afebrile, off oxygen, and eating well after 48 hours, with negative repeated blood cultures. All family members were treated with topical permethrin 5% (two doses 1 week apart), and children with skin sores received a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin, with excellent response. Household clothes, linen, and furniture were disinfected, and rooms treated with insecticide. The patient returned to the community after 3 weeks with no residual hyperkeratosis or shedding and continues regular follow-up.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was crusted scabies, caused by Sarcoptes scabiei infestation, complicated by secondary bacterial sepsis due to community-acquired MRSA (Staphylococcus aureus). This was supported by clinical presentation with a widespread exfoliative rash and systemic unwellness, confirmation of scabies mites and eggs on skin scrapings, and positive blood cultures for MRSA, with good response to specific anti-scabies treatment and vancomycin.
